routes.description: Establish a historical core of Jesus' death, burial or empty tomb, and postmortem appearances, then show that bodily resurrection explains that core within an adequately supported theistic framework.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical premises are sufficiently supported, bodily resurrection accounts for them more adequately than the live natural alternatives, and objections concerning testimony, prior probability, and miracle attribution do not defeat the inference.

motionBridge.description: Connect the supported historical core and comparative explanation directly to the rational conclusion that Jesus bodily rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Establish Jesus' death and burial or empty tomb together with reported postmortem experiences sufficiently robust to require explanation.
Show that the appearance and resurrection traditions concern a transformed physical body rather than only an inward or immaterial experience.
Show that hallucination, removal, survival, fraud, legend, and combinations of such accounts do not explain the historical core as adequately.
Provide sufficient background warrant for divine action and connect that framework specifically to Jesus so resurrection is an admissible historical explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the early, eyewitness-linked, and mutually reinforcing character of the traditions used to establish the historical premises.
Use claimed anomalous or survival evidence to challenge strict naturalistic exclusion without treating that evidence itself as proof of resurrection.

routes.description: Show that the partisan and limited historical record does not distinguish bodily resurrection from visionary, removal, error-based, or presently unreconstructable alternatives under an appropriate standard for miracle attribution.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if indispensable historical or bodily premises remain uncertain, the evidence remains underdetermined by available alternatives, or justified background beliefs about supernatural agency are insufficient to make resurrection the warranted conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Connect unresolved historical and epistemic underdetermination directly to the conclusion that bodily resurrection is not established by the evidence.

centralBridges.description: Show that chronology, partisan sourcing, limited independent testimony, and textual ambiguity constrain the historical premises available for the resurrection inference.
Show that grief visions, hallucination, body removal, error, or combinations of ordinary possibilities can resist the resurrection inference without a complete reconstruction.
Challenge whether reported seeing, touching, and spiritual-body language establish an externally observable and coherent bodily resurrection.
Require independently justified beliefs about a supernatural agent, its nature, and its intentions before unexplained evidence may rationally be attributed to miracle.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Treat inability to reconstruct a distant event as a reason for a tentative conclusion rather than as affirmative support for resurrection.
Require appropriate repeatability or independent validation before anomalous perception reports alter the background case for supernatural survival.

sections.title: Historical Sources and Early Tradition
sections.rationale: The dating, provenance, independence, and eyewitness linkage of Pauline, creedal, Gospel, and non-Christian material determine the evidential foundation available to both burden routes.

sections.title: Death, Burial, and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: Actual death and the disposition of Jesus' body are indispensable to bodily resurrection, while the empty-tomb evidence and ordinary removal possibilities shape what requires explanation.

sections.title: Appearances and Psychological Alternatives
sections.rationale: The reported experiences of disciples, groups, Paul, and other converts form the principal experiential basis of the case and the principal ground for visionary or hallucination accounts.

sections.title: Nature of the Resurrection Body
sections.rationale: Contact narratives, sensory reports, eating accounts, and Pauline spiritual-body language bear directly on whether the traditions support bodily resurrection rather than an immaterial manifestation.

sections.title: Comparative Explanation and Burden of Reconstruction
sections.rationale: The motion turns partly on whether resurrection must outperform a complete natural reconstruction or whether unresolved ordinary possibilities are enough to leave the evidence underdetermined.

sections.title: Miracle Priors and Worldview Evidence
sections.rationale: Prior beliefs about God, divine intention, natural law, anomalous perception, and survival after death affect when historical evidence can rationally support a specifically miraculous conclusion.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: The historical core presented for explanation includes transformative appearance experiences by the disciples and the conversions of James and Paul.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Habermas to present his case, and this uninterrupted answer precedes the handoff to Flew.

response.rationale: This constructive move identifies the principal reported appearances and conversions that form the experiential part of the historical core requiring explanation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly supplies a central historical premise, though the excerpt compresses the supporting documentation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable as a report about experiences believed to be appearances, rather than an assertion that resurrection is already proven.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The wording distinguishes the participants' beliefs from the truth of those beliefs and presents the material as a shared historical starting point.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reported transformations and conversions coherently identify phenomena needing explanation, with only the evidential bridge left compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific disciples, James, and Paul are identified, but the excerpt relies partly on asserted scholarly common ground without representative documentation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central historical-core bridge by identifying the principal postmortem experiences and resulting transformations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents affirmative historical material without engaging a sufficiently developed live alternative interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names James and Paul, describes their prior skepticism or opposition, and says they converted through experiences they believed were appearances.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Agreement on proposed facts does not overcome an evidential record marked by uncertain chronology, partisan documents, absent Gospel eyewitnesses, and limited independent testimony.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Flew by name, and Flew expressly responds to Habermas's facts before the moderator asks Gary for an answer.

components.text: Whether the proposed appearance facts rest on a sufficiently reliable historical record.
Whether scholarly agreement on a list of facts supplies adequate independent evidential support.

response.rationale: Flew directly challenges the evidential foundation of the proposed historical core by citing uncertain chronology, partisan documents, absent Gospel eyewitnesses, and limited independent testimony.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the reliability premise underlying the proposed facts and supplies several source-specific objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limitations are stated as constraints on evidential adequacy rather than as proof that every reported event is false.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The skeptical conclusion generally fits the listed limitations, though the emphasis on unknown exact chronology somewhat overstates that consideration's force.

charity.alternative: The appearance facts may remain historically credible despite partisan and incomplete surviving sources.
charity.decisiveQualification: Agreement and early tradition do not by themselves establish independence or eyewitness access.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from source limitations to reduced confidence is coherent, although exact dating is not itself indispensable to the core claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete limitations are supplied, but the excerpt does not document their extent or compare the strongest source-proximity case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the central bridge concerning chronology, partisan sourcing, eyewitness access, and independent testimony.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges agreement on proposed facts but fairly insists that agreement does not remove the underlying source limitations.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly calls the evidential situation unsatisfactory, notes uncertainty about chronology, and emphasizes that the evidence is document-based.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: The First Corinthians 15 tradition is early, was received and transmitted by Paul, and is linked through his Jerusalem visit to Peter and James.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests an example from Gary's preceding answer, and the sustained first-person exposition is followed by a direct question to Tony.

components.text: Whether early Pauline tradition provides source proximity despite the broader record's limitations.
Whether the tradition can be linked to eyewitness-associated figures Peter and James.

response.rationale: Habermas answers the source-proximity objection with a dated Pauline text, technical transmission language, and an argued Jerusalem link to Peter and James.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly addresses chronology and eyewitness linkage with specific textual and biographical claims, while independence remains less developed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The text clearly separates the date of First Corinthians from the inferred earlier reception of its transmitted material.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The key Jerusalem-source inference is framed as most likely rather than certain, matching the indirect nature of the reconstruction.

charity.alternative: Early Pauline transmission can still be partisan, dependent, or insufficiently independent.
charity.decisiveQualification: Early linkage improves proximity but does not alone establish every Gospel detail or full source independence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Dating, transmission terminology, and the Jerusalem visit form a coherent chain, with one bounded implicit bridge about the creed's source.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites a specific passage, technical terms, and named contacts, but the inference that Peter and James supplied the material remains indirect.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It sits at the top of the subsidiary source-proximity tier because it directly supplies early dating and eyewitness-associated transmission.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly answers proximity and eyewitness linkage, though it does not fully absorb the broader objection about partisan dependence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt dates First Corinthians, quotes Paul's received-and-delivered terminology, identifies it as transmission language, and infers reception in Jerusalem.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The disciples' reported experiences are plausibly grief-related visions with no externally visible object rather than encounters with a bodily risen Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Tony for his naturalistic theory, and the answer ends before the moderator introduces a related publication.

components.text: Whether the disciples' appearance experiences require an external risen body as their object.
Whether grief-related experiences offer an ordinary explanation of the reported appearances.

response.rationale: Flew accepts that experiences occurred but directly supplies grief visions as an alternative explanation and denies that an externally observable object was present.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the explanatory significance of the appearance experiences, though it does not address James or Paul.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grief-vision proposal is clear for bereaved disciples, but its scope across different disciples and group reports is left somewhat unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is presented as a natural interpretation supported by an ordinary analogy, without claiming a complete reconstruction of all appearances.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Grief visions coherently explain some bereavement experiences, though extending them to all relevant witnesses and circumstances requires further bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The familiar bereavement analogy supplies some support, but no representative evidence addresses groups, varied witnesses, or the specific ancient reports.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly preserves a principal natural alternative to the disciples' appearances, an indispensable comparative issue.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances an alternative explanation but does not substantially interpret or characterize a developed opposing psychological account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls such grief experiences fairly common, analogizes them to seeing a deceased close relative, and denies an external object.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Conversion disorder and grief hallucinations do not jointly explain Paul and the disciples because the proposed conditions lack evidence and do not fit the varied groups, circumstances, and transformations.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Gary whether the proposed psychological explanations work, and Gary delivers a continuous rebuttal until Flew is invited to respond.

components.text: Whether grief hallucinations fit the relevant disciples and reported circumstances.
Whether the proposed psychological account can also explain Paul and the diversity of cases.

response.rationale: Habermas directly tests the proposed psychological explanations against Paul, the disciples, the required conditions, and the absence of evidence for the motivations attributed to Paul.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the fit and evidential premises of the grief-vision account across the relevant witness categories.

precisionFindings.rationale: The overall comparative claim is recoverable, although several psychological labels and proposed disorders are compressed in rapid succession.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The detailed mismatch case supports strong skepticism, but the categorical rhetoric goes somewhat beyond what the excerpt's cited psychological assertions establish.

charity.alternative: Different psychological mechanisms could apply to Paul and to bereaved disciples without one uniform disorder.
charity.decisiveQualification: A composite account still needs evidence that each mechanism fits its assigned witness and circumstances.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Testing necessary conditions against distinct witnesses is a strong comparative method, with some psychological premises left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides case-specific mismatch claims and identifies absent evidence for Paul's alleged motivation, but specialist claims receive limited documentation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central task of defeating principal psychological alternatives across Paul, disciples, and varied circumstances.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes multiple proposed mechanisms and fairly presses their case-specific evidential requirements rather than treating them as one crude theory.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that the proposed circumstances do not apply to Paul, lists multiple required psychological conditions, and denies evidence that Paul wanted conversion.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Against extensive historical ignorance and severely limited non-Christian evidence, the reasonable conclusion is a tentative natural interpretation rather than a publicly observable physical resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: A question characterizes the psychological account as hypothesis, after which Flew answers in his distinctive first-person skeptical voice until the moderator intervenes.

components.text: Whether failure of particular psychological theories warrants the positive resurrection inference.
Whether limited evidence can distinguish an externally visible physical body from a tentative natural interpretation.

response.rationale: Flew justifies replacing a demand for a complete psychological reconstruction with the more limited demand for historical restraint under extensive ignorance, preserving the issue of what the evidence warrants.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe directly addresses the inferential consequence of incomplete natural accounts, although it supplies little detail about the preferred natural interpretation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is expressly tentative and scoped to what can reasonably be inferred from the limited historical evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cautious force fits the appeal to extensive ignorance and avoids asserting a detailed natural reconstruction unsupported by the record.

charity.alternative: The convergence of appearance evidence may rationally favor a physical resurrection despite historical gaps.
charity.decisiveQualification: Comparative superiority still requires enough evidence to distinguish physical resurrection from unresolved ordinary possibilities.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from severe underdetermination to a tentative conclusion is coherent and avoids the false demand for a complete rival narrative.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt identifies general historical ignorance and limited evidence, but it does not specifically demonstrate the extent of each claimed evidential gap.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly connects historical and explanatory underdetermination to the motion-level conclusion that bodily resurrection is not established.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not deny that evidence exists; it fairly disputes how far that evidence can carry a public physical-body conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stresses enormous background ignorance, limits the reasonable aim to suggesting an interpretation, and rejects postulating a publicly visible physical body.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The Thomas narrative does not establish bodily contact because it reports an invitation to touch and subsequent sight but does not clearly report that Thomas actually touched Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Tony whether he accepts the four facts, and Flew's answer about Thomas continues until Gary is expressly asked to respond.

components.text: Whether transformative appearance experiences generally establish a bodily encounter.

response.rationale: The textual observation about Thomas bears on bodily interpretation, but it does not contact the broader historical-core claim's decisive component concerning the existence and transformation of the reported experiences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is relevant contrary material about bodily contact, but it does not answer the broader appearance-core component of the selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is narrowly and clearly limited to what the Thomas narrative does and does not explicitly report.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The wording appropriately says the text does not clearly report touching rather than claiming that touching certainly never occurred.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between an invitation to touch and a report that touching occurred is explicit, valid, and narrowly consequential.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument closely tracks the described narrative sequence, though the excerpt does not quote the complete surrounding passage for verification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the central challenge to bodily interpretation, but only through one bounded narrative ambiguity rather than the whole bodily case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move makes a narrow textual observation without engaging a developed alternative reading strongly enough for a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes Jesus' reported invitation from any explicit report that Thomas actually placed his hands in the wounds.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Johannine reports of seeing and touching, together with Luke's flesh-and-bones language and eating scene, support a tangible physical resurrection body rather than a ghostly manifestation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers Flew's complaint about sparse touch evidence by citing Johannine and Lucan material, followed immediately by Flew's skeptical rejoinder.

components.text: Whether the textual tradition contains affirmative seeing and touching evidence despite the Thomas ambiguity.
Whether the traditions describe a tangible physical body rather than an unobservable manifestation.

response.rationale: Habermas answers the narrow Thomas objection by broadening to Johannine touch language and Luke's invitation, flesh-and-bones context, and eating report as cumulative sensory evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive bodily-evidence issue with several specific texts, though it does not fully resolve the narrow fact that Thomas's touch is unreported.

precisionFindings.rationale: The physical-body conclusion is clear, but the move only implicitly qualifies differences among the cited narratives and speakers.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Multiple sensory motifs support a strong textual conclusion, with a bounded implicit caveat about historicity and narrative independence.

charity.alternative: Thomas may not have touched Jesus even if other passages use touch and eating language.
charity.decisiveQualification: The broader bodily case need not depend exclusively on Thomas actually completing the invited contact.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Seeing, touching, flesh-and-bones language, and eating coherently support tangibility, subject to one bounded bridge from texts to events.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several specific narrative features are cited, but their historical reliability and independence are not defended within this move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable central bridge from appearance traditions to the bodily character of the claimed resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the narrow Thomas ambiguity while fairly showing why other sensory reports could independently bear the bodily inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites hands touching, Luke's invitation to touch rather than regard Jesus as a ghost, eating, and repeated seeing and touching.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Calling a body spiritual appears incoherent because an immaterial substance has no identifiable characteristics and is not genuinely a body.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Flew to answer, and the ensuing first-person objection continues until the next moderator question.

components.text: Whether the proposed resurrection body is conceptually coherent when also described as spiritual.
Whether calling something immaterial supplies characteristics compatible with genuine embodiment.

response.rationale: Flew directly challenges the conceptual bridge between the sensory physical-body claim and spiritual-body terminology by arguing that immateriality supplies no bodily characteristics.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly contacts the coherence of the claimed kind of body, although it assumes that spiritual means immaterial.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is clear, but the equivalence between spiritual and immaterial is offered as an implicit interpretive premise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual concern is legitimate, but saying an immaterial substance is nothing somewhat overstates what the semantic premise establishes.

charity.alternative: Spiritual body may mean a body transformed or governed by spirit rather than an immaterial object.
charity.decisiveQualification: The term still requires a positive account showing how transformed embodiment retains identifiable bodily characteristics.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows if spiritual means immaterial, but that central equivalence is disputed and insufficiently defended in the move.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument rests mainly on a semantic and metaphysical assertion without textual support for its interpretation of spiritual-body language.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central challenge to whether the asserted resurrection body is conceptually coherent and genuinely bodily.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection identifies a real explanatory demand but materially narrows the live Pauline interpretation by treating spiritual as simply immaterial.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt equates spiritual with immaterial, argues immateriality supplies no identifiable characteristic, and concludes that a spiritual body is not a body.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Paul's spiritual-body language denotes a transformed body rather than a disembodied spirit, as clarified by his description of bodily transformation in Philippians 3.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator's exchange ends with agreement, after which Habermas explicitly addresses Tony and interprets the Pauline passages in sequence.

components.text: Whether Paul's spiritual-body language entails an immaterial or disembodied entity.
Whether Philippians 3 supplies a positive transformed-body interpretation that defeats the alleged incoherence.

response.rationale: Habermas identifies the objection's decisive semantic premise as anachronistic, invokes Philippians 3 as Pauline clarification, and states the defeating consequence that spiritual need not mean nonphysical.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly diagnoses the disputed equivalence and supplies an intratextual reason for reading spiritual body as transformed embodiment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition clearly distinguishes transformed embodiment from a wispy or disembodied spirit and identifies the texts used for interpretation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The interpretation is advocated firmly but framed as the speaker's reading, appropriately acknowledging the inferential nature of the cross-textual argument.

charity.alternative: Spiritual body could remain conceptually obscure even if it is not wholly disembodied.
charity.decisiveQualification: Philippians 3 supports transformation, but a complete account of the transformed body's properties is still absent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move explicitly attacks the key equivocation and uses one Pauline passage to clarify another, leaving only bounded metaphysical detail implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies a specific intratextual comparison, though the relevant Philippians wording and competing exegesis are not fully presented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central bodily-character bridge by explaining why spiritual-body language need not imply disembodiment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly addresses the strongest semantic objection through Pauline context while leaving the residual metaphysical details unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects a modern reading of spiritual as wispy or nonphysical and treats Philippians 3 as commentary on First Corinthians 15.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Whether belief in an alleged miracle is rational depends on antecedent beliefs, so the same resurrection reports need not rationally support a miracle for someone who initially suspects error.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Tony by name, and Flew answers in the first person by contrasting his own priors with those of Jews and Christians.

components.text: Whether Pauline spiritual-body language coherently denotes transformed physical embodiment.

response.rationale: The discussion of antecedent beliefs is important to miracle rationality but does not contact the selected target's decisive textual and conceptual question about transformed embodiment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is issue-bearing contrary material at the worldview level, yet it is not an answer to the bodily-language component of the legal target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional claim about rational response under differing priors is clearly stated and expressly allows that persuasion remains possible.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity concerns dependence on prior beliefs, not impossibility of miracle evidence, and the speaker explicitly allows sufficiently spectacular evidence to persuade.

charity.alternative: Strong resurrection evidence could rationally revise initially skeptical priors.
charity.decisiveQualification: Prior dependence does not make priors unrevisable; it changes the evidential threshold and comparative assessment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional relation between antecedent beliefs and evidential thresholds is explicit, consistent, and avoids absolute exclusion of miracles.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic principle is plausibly illustrated by contrasting prior outlooks, though no fuller account of justified prior formation is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central requirement that miracle attribution be evaluated against independently assessable antecedent beliefs.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly acknowledges possible persuasion and therefore handles the strongest evidence-revision alternative with its decisive qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that rational response depends on prior belief, describes an initial error presumption, and allows sufficiently spectacular evidence to overcome it.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Jesus' death by crucifixion is supported cumulatively by medical considerations, broad critical acceptance, non-Christian attestations, and Paul's early preaching.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Habermas for evidence of death and outside sources, and the answer identifies medical, scholarly, extrabiblical, and Pauline support.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes actual death as an indispensable part of the historical core through several claimed evidential streams rather than relying on one source.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly supplies a central historical premise with a clearly cumulative structure and several named support types.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is a clear cumulative historical claim about death by crucifixion, with stable evidential categories and no obscuring scope shift.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The force fits the convergence of medical, critical, extrabiblical, and early Pauline considerations offered for a widely bounded historical premise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple independent types of support coherently converge on the death premise, with no material contradiction or missing validity bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several representative support categories and named critical scholars are given, though medical and extrabiblical materials are not fully documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Actual death is indispensable to the central historical core and is addressed directly through a broad cumulative argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents a constructive cumulative case without engaging a developed survival or mistaken-death alternative in this span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes medical data, critical scholarship, extrabiblical evidence, and named skeptical scholars who regard crucifixion as exceptionally secure.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Early attestation, hostile acknowledgment, proclamation in Jerusalem, and women as culturally unlikely invented witnesses jointly support the empty tomb.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests evidence that the tomb was empty, and Habermas enumerates four reasons before explicitly asking Flew to respond to them.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies four cumulative considerations for the empty tomb, directly addressing the bodily disposition component of the historical core.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly enumerates multiple mutually reinforcing reasons aimed at an indispensable historical premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly cumulative, so no single consideration is misleadingly presented as independently conclusive.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The convergence warrants significant confidence, but hostile acknowledgment and Jerusalem proclamation require additional assumptions not fully stated here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The four considerations coherently converge, though the Jerusalem and hostile-acknowledgment inferences each retain compressed background assumptions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers several specific evidential lines, but their independence, exact sources, and strongest rival interpretations are not fully defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central historical-core bridge by arguing for the empty tomb through early, hostile, geographic, and witness evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move constructs an affirmative empty-tomb case but does not directly develop or assess a specific removal or legendary alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies women witnesses, early Pauline attestation, Jewish acknowledgment, and Jerusalem proclamation as mutually reinforcing empty-tomb considerations.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Without independent witnesses, many ordinary removals of a body remain possible, and the distant historical episode cannot be reliably reconstructed from the available evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator identifies the question as Flew's and Flew answers in his characteristic first-person form before the moderator turns back to Gary.

components.text: Whether the empty-tomb evidence excludes ordinary removal of the body.
Whether the available witnesses and distant record permit a reliable reconstruction of the body's disposition.

response.rationale: Flew directly answers the empty-tomb case by stressing absent independent witnesses, multiple ordinary removal possibilities, and the limits on reconstructing the distant event.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the underdetermination of the empty-tomb inference, although it does not individually answer each of the four cumulative considerations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly claims underdetermination and inability to reconstruct, not affirmative proof of any particular removal scenario.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited force matches the evidence offered: ordinary removal remains possible, while no complete account is asserted.

charity.alternative: The four cumulative considerations may make removal substantially less likely even without modern independent witnesses.
charity.decisiveQualification: Their force still depends on source reliability and does not logically exclude unknown ordinary removal routes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from absent independent observation and multiple possible removals to underdetermination is coherent and appropriately limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The source limitation is concrete, but the assertion of many removal routes remains generic and receives no representative historical comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly preserves a central natural alternative concerning bodily disposition and attacks the inference from emptiness to resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the cumulative evidence's possible force while fairly insisting that it does not yield a unique reconstruction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites the lack of independent witnesses, states that bodies can be removed in many ways, and disclaims a complete reconstruction.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Naturalistic alternatives fail to explain the evidence as a unified whole and require multiplying separate accounts for Jesus' death, the disciples' appearances, Paul's experience, and the empty tomb.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Gary to survey naturalistic accounts, and Habermas proceeds through swoon, fraud, hallucination, legend, and combined explanations.

components.text: Whether merely possible body removals explain the evidential set as a unified whole.
Whether one grief-hallucination account fits both Paul and the disciples.
Whether historical restraint alone answers the comparative explanatory demand.

response.rationale: Habermas directly compares the principal natural accounts and argues that combining distinct explanations for death, appearances, Paul, and the tomb reduces their unified explanatory adequacy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts several live alternatives and their joint explanatory burden, though it compresses comparison of their independent probabilities.

precisionFindings.rationale: The unified-explanation claim is clear, with an implicit qualification that multiple mechanisms are objectionable because of evidential fit rather than mere numerical plurality.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The multiplication concern has real comparative force, but counting theories does not by itself establish that a composite account is less probable.

charity.alternative: Different ordinary causes may independently explain different parts of a heterogeneous evidential set.
charity.decisiveQualification: Plurality is not automatically ad hoc; the relevant question is each component's fit, prior plausibility, and joint probability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand for unified fit is relevant, but the inference from several mechanisms to comparative failure leaves a material probability bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move surveys several named theories and identifies concrete coverage gaps, though it does not quantify or seriously compare composite alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central burden of defeating principal alternatives by testing their coverage of the entire historical set.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move considers composite alternatives but materially understates the legitimate possibility that heterogeneous effects have heterogeneous causes.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that hallucination leaves the empty tomb and requires different forms for Paul and the disciples, within a wider survey of natural accounts.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: A satisfactory complete naturalistic reconstruction may be unavailable, while hallucination can still explain much of the appearance evidence even though it leaves the empty tomb unexplained.
moves.attributionBasis: Flew interrupts the characterization of his position with a first-person clarification, and the moderator then immediately asks him a new question.

components.text: Whether rejecting resurrection requires a satisfactory complete naturalistic reconstruction.
Whether hallucination may retain partial explanatory value despite leaving the empty tomb unexplained.

response.rationale: Flew expressly rejects the demand for a complete rival, substitutes the evidential question of whether resurrection is established, and candidly specifies both hallucination's coverage and its empty-tomb limitation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe directly addresses the disputed burden, preserves the legitimate comparative issue, and explicitly acknowledges the alternative's principal gap.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim precisely distinguishes lacking a complete natural account from retaining a partial explanation for some appearance evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim fits the conceded incompleteness and does not overstate hallucination as an explanation of the empty tomb.

charity.alternative: A unified resurrection account may be preferable to several incomplete natural explanations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Preference for unity does not shift the positive burden or make an incomplete rival necessary for withholding the resurrection conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between defeating a positive inference and supplying a complete contrary history is explicit, valid, and consistently maintained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The burden principle is strongly stated and the explanatory limitation candidly identified, though hallucination's claimed coverage remains only broadly supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion-level underdetermination conclusion by clarifying that no complete rival reconstruction is required.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately represents the unification challenge and answers it while expressly conceding the natural account's strongest unresolved datum.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies offering a satisfactory complete natural account, says hallucination covers much of the data, and concedes no explanation for the empty tomb.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Evidence for God, present-day anomalies, and survival after death can alter the relevant background assumptions and raise the prior plausibility of resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Habermas to answer, and Flew's response begins immediately after this sustained turn.

components.text: Whether background evidence can rationally alter initially skeptical miracle priors.
Whether evidence for God, present anomalies, and survival makes resurrection antecedently less improbable.

response.rationale: Habermas directly accepts the relevance of priors and answers by proposing several bodies of background evidence that could raise the prior plausibility of divine action and survival.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the prior-probability demand with relevant evidence categories, though their actual strength is only sketched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The probabilistic function of the evidence is clear, although present-day anomalies and survival evidence remain broad, heterogeneous categories.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional claim that God's existence would raise the prior is fitting, but the excerpt does not establish that the cited background evidence is sufficiently strong.

charity.alternative: Skeptical priors may remain justified if anomaly and survival reports lack independent validation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Merely naming background evidence does not establish its reliability or connect a possible deity specifically to resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The Bayesian-style direction of the argument is coherent, with a material bridge remaining from generic anomalies to resurrection-specific prior probability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several evidence categories and a conditional concession are named, but representative cases, validation, and independence are not adequately supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central miracle-framework bridge by attempting to supply background warrant that could change relevant priors.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply correctly recognizes the prior-evidence demand but gives limited attention to the strongest validation and agent-specific objections.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes evidence for God, near-death experiences, present miracles, and Flew's earlier conditional statement that God's existence would raise resurrection likelihood.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: A sufficiently rich convergence of bodily identification, personal interaction, and multiple-witness evidence can rationally overcome the ordinary presumption that a dead person remains dead.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the resurrection question to Gary, who answers continuously until inviting Tony's response.

components.text: Whether sufficiently rich positive evidence can establish resurrection without demanding a complete natural rival.
Whether identification and multiple-witness evidence can overcome the ordinary presumption of continued death.

response.rationale: Habermas answers restraint and prior skepticism by describing a threshold at which convergent identification, interaction, death confirmation, and witness evidence could positively overcome the ordinary presumption.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the evidential-threshold issue directly, though the illustrative hypothetical is not itself evidence that the historical case reaches that threshold.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly conditional on sufficiently rich convergent evidence and does not say that every surprising report defeats the presumption.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional possibility is well matched to the hypothetical illustration and avoids claiming that the illustration alone proves the historical application.

charity.alternative: No complete natural rival is required if the positive resurrection evidence remains insufficient.
charity.decisiveQualification: That burden principle remains correct; the pro side must independently show that its actual convergence crosses the warranted threshold.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The hypothetical coherently shows that priors are defeasible by convergence, with one important bridge from the analogy to the ancient evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The illustration clarifies a valid evidential principle, but it supplies modern hypothetical features not independently established for the historical reports.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the motion-level claim of unavoidable underdetermination by articulating how convergent evidence could rationally establish resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly preserves the positive burden and explains how evidence could meet it rather than simply demanding a rival reconstruction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt constructs a case involving prior death confirmation, personal recognition, physical interaction, photographs, and consideration of ordinary mistaken-identity options.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Miracle evidence becomes rational only against justified prior beliefs about a supernatural agent's existence, nature, and intentions.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas asks Tony for his view, and Flew responds in the first person until Habermas resumes the theological application.

components.text: Whether generic background anomalies suffice without justified beliefs about a supernatural agent.
Whether unexplained convergent evidence can rationally be attributed specifically to miraculous agency.

response.rationale: Flew directly refines the prior-evidence demand: miracle attribution requires justified beliefs not merely about anomaly but about a supernatural agent's existence, character, and intentions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the missing agent-specific bridge and states the additional theological warrant required for miracle attribution.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional requirement is clearly recoverable and distinguishes human practical impossibility from justified attribution to supernatural agency.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity is narrowly attached to rational miracle attribution, while the move expressly allows that evidence for miracle can exist.

charity.alternative: Exceptionally strong event evidence might itself contribute to justified belief in supernatural agency.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even then, inferring this agent and intention requires more than labeling an event unexplained or humanly impossible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between anomaly, human impossibility, and intentional supernatural action is explicit and identifies the decisive attribution bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic requirement is well motivated conceptually, though the move does not fully defend how much independent theology is necessary.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central bridge requiring justified prior theology before assigning unexplained historical evidence to miracle.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows miracle evidence in principle and fairly locates the remaining burden in agent-specific theological justification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines miracle in relation to natural law and human practical impossibility, then requires justified prior beliefs concerning a supernatural being.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Jesus' claims connect him to Mosaic theism, so a well-supported resurrection would function as divine authentication of the identity he claimed.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas explicitly refers back to the prior segment and develops the Jesus-specific implication before the moderator closes the segment.

components.text: Whether the proposed miracle can be connected to a specific supernatural agent and intention.
Whether Jesus' claims and Mosaic-theistic context provide an authentication framework for resurrection.

response.rationale: Habermas directly supplies the requested agent-specific link by connecting Jesus' identity claims to Mosaic theism and interpreting resurrection as divine authentication of those claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts supernatural identity and intention, though it assumes rather than independently establishes the Mosaic-theistic framework.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is clearly conditional on a well-supported resurrection and identifies both the relevant tradition and the claimed authentication function.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional authentication inference has force, but the assertion that God would not raise a heretic leaves divine intention insufficiently defended.

charity.alternative: Even if resurrection occurred, its divine source and intended endorsement of every identity claim might remain uncertain.
charity.decisiveQualification: Authentication requires justified Mosaic theism plus a warranted premise about what such a God would intend by resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional chain is intelligible, but it leaves a material bridge from resurrection by God to endorsement of the claimant's asserted identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Jesus' titles and theological setting are identified, but Mosaic theism, divine causation, and the nonauthentication-of-heretics premise remain asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central miracle-framework bridge by connecting the alleged event to a specific tradition, claimant, and divine purpose.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply squarely addresses the alternative but compresses the decisive divine-intention premise into an asserted theological maxim.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt links Jesus' Son of God and Son of Man claims to Mosaic tradition and argues that resurrection would authenticate rather than condemn him.
